title: Neurofibromatosis
subject: Pathology
summary: Neurofibromatosis is a genetic disorder of neural crest cells, presenting with café‑au‑lait spots, neurofibromas and optic gliomas. NF1 is most common, NF2 involves vestibular schwannomas, and schwannomatosis is a distinct entity.

sections.p: Neurofibromatosis refers to three distinct hereditary syndromes: NF1 (chromosome 17), NF2 (chromosome 22) and schwannomatosis. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria and, when available, genetic testing.
b: NF1: 6+ café‑au‑lait macules >5 mm (children) or >15 mm (adults), 2+ neurofibromas, axillary/inguinal freckling, optic glioma, Lisch nodules, pheochromocytoma, bony dysplasia
NF2: bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas, schwannomas of spinal roots
Schwannomatosis: multiple schwannomas without vestibular involvement, no CNS tumors

sections.p: NF1 is staged by the NIH criteria: mild (few cutaneous lesions), moderate (multiple neurofibromas, optic glioma), severe (multiple CNS tumors, skeletal abnormalities).
Autosomal dominant mutations in NF1, NF2 or SMARCB1/ LZTR1 genes. De novo mutations occur in ~50% of cases. In low‑resource settings, consanguinity may increase recurrence.

Early childhood: café‑au‑lait macules, axillary freckling. Adolescence: cutaneous neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma symptoms (blurred vision). Adults: spinal neurofibromas, hearing loss (NF2).
b: Plexiform neurofibroma – disfiguring, risk of malignant transformation

sections.p: Use available resources; prioritize imaging and basic labs.

t.b: Detects optic glioma, vestibular schwannoma, spinal neurofibromas; absence suggests other causes
Screen for pheochromocytoma if hypertension present
Rule out electrolyte disturbances from adrenal tumors
Confirms diagnosis when clinical criteria equivocal

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour, optic pathway glioma causing blindness, pheochromocytoma crisis, spinal cord compression.
Multidisciplinary care: surveillance, symptomatic treatment, surgery when indicated. Avoid drugs that increase bleeding risk or interact with anaesthesia.
b: Regular ophthalmology review for optic glioma
Neurosurgical referral for symptomatic spinal neurofibromas

sections.p: Annual review of growth, vision, hearing, blood pressure. Genetic counselling for families. No preventive cure; early detection of complications improves outcomes.
Tuberous sclerosis (café‑au‑lait spots, seizures), Sturge‑Weber syndrome (port‑wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma), neurofibromatosis type 1 vs. schwannomatosis (absence of vestibular schwannoma).
Café‑au‑lait spots may appear in other dermatoses; small neurofibromas can be missed on physical exam; MRI may not detect small peripheral lesions.

whenToSeekHelp: Neurological deficit suggesting spinal cord compression

faq.q: What is the most common mutation in NF1?
faq.a: A nonsense or missense mutation in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17.
Yes, cognitive impairment and attention deficits are common in NF1.

faq.q: Is there a cure for neurofibromatosis?
faq.a: No, treatment is supportive and aimed at managing complications.

exam: A 12‑year‑old presents with multiple café‑au‑lait spots and axillary freckling – what is the next best investigation? — MRI brain to screen for optic glioma; if unavailable, ophthalmology review.
A 35‑year‑old with NF2 has bilateral tinnitus and hearing loss – which tumour is most likely? — Vestibular schwannoma; explain why other CNS tumours are less likely.
A patient with NF1 develops sudden severe headache and hypertension – what is the immediate concern? — Pheochromocytoma crisis; start alpha‑blockade before beta‑blocker.
A plexiform neurofibroma suddenly enlarges – what complication should you suspect? — Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour; urgent imaging and referral.
During a ward round you note a patient with NF1 has a new visual disturbance – what is the most urgent step? — Ophthalmology assessment for optic pathway glioma.
A patient with NF1 is scheduled for spinal surgery – what peri‑operative medication should be avoided? — Anticoagulants that increase bleeding risk; use careful haemostasis.
A child with NF1 has a café‑au‑lait spot <5 mm – does this meet diagnostic criteria? — No, need 6+ spots >5 mm or >15 mm in adults.
A patient with NF2 has a solitary mass on the neck – is this likely part of NF2? — Unlikely; NF2 usually has multiple bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
